Resolved, that it is expedient to extend the time within which the Saint John and Quebec Railway Company is to complete the construction and equipment of its line of railway from a point at or near Centreville, in the county of Carleton, to a point at or near Andover, in the County of Victoria, to the thirty-first day of December, 1927, both with respect to the agreement entered into under the authority of section three of The Saint John and Quebec Railway Act, 1916, and also with respect to the subsidy agreement made under the authority of section six of the said Act: Provided that the said extension shall only be granted with respect to the first named agreement after the consent of His Majesty on behalf of the Province of New Brunswick has been obtained.

maintopic: ST. JOHN AND QUEBEC RAILWAY CENTREVILLE-ANDOVER BRANCH
speechtext: I would like to ask-

maintopic: ST. JOHN AND QUEBEC RAILWAY CENTREVILLE-ANDOVER BRANCH

maintopic: ST. JOHN AND QUEBEC RAILWAY CENTREVILLE-ANDOVER BRANCH
speechtext:
I would like to ask whether this is simply a formal extenson to take advantage of some happier financial times, or whether it is the intention of both governments that the work shall be proceeded with. Railway matters are being discussed between them so frequently that it would be indeed very desirable if any policy could be enunciated by which this road would be carried to its originally intended termini, and if arrangements could also be made with the Canadian Pacific by which their line now running, through the state of Maine could be diverted, so that all the traffic upon the western side of New Brunswick, as well as the traffic of the Canadian Pacific might be carried by joint operation of this line with its better construction and better grades. So much of this line as has been constructed has been built to conform to the National Transcontinental grade. I do not intend to take up much time in discussing the unfortunate history of the road, the completion of which was prevented by the advent of the war, nor the unfortunate lack of earning power, because the road is not complete, which results every four years in an addition of $1,000,000 to the bonded debt of the little province of New Brunswick. The average deficit is about $250,000 a year. The province is not able to sustain that deficit out of income, and therefore each year it capitalizes it, involving a further heavy obligation; and I am stating the

St. John and Quebec Railway
matter fairly when I say that every four years there is, in round numbers, an addition of $1,000,000 to our bonded debt. I believe that that burden could be lifted from the province if by the joint operation of the Dominion and the local governments this road were carried to completion. It would be a much more vital and intensely more useful part of the government system than the National Transcontinental which was cut "slash-ways" through the province of New Brunswick and is, taking it at the present time, almost idle-in fact, it is scarcely operating at all. This road will run through a splendid country, will serve a number of thriving communities, and I believe it would be a very good opportunity for the minister to demonstrate the principle of joint operation and thereby reduce the expenses of both the great railway systems.
I should like the minister when answering to kindly give me information as to whether there is anything real in the sugestions we have had in New Brunswick that the Canadian National system is about to take over the St. John Valley railway. A return was asked for in this House and it was filed some time ago, but with the exception of the correspondence that took place between the governments about the time of the construction of that railway, and a later memorandum which places the views of the province very dearly indeed-having been sent forward by Premier Foster shortly after his accession to office about eight years ago-there is on file. Statements have been made _ by public men in New Brunswick that this is a matter for oral negotiation. Now, we m New Brunswick would like to know just what has been said on the subject-how far the oral negotiations have proceeded, what is the outlook for a settlement, and what settlement mav be arrived at in this matter which is one of very great interest to the people ol the whole province.

maintopic: ST. JOHN AND QUEBEC RAILWAY CENTREVILLE-ANDOVER BRANCH
speechtext:
There is another
feature of this matter that is possibly as important as those advanced, and the reasons advanced are valid and good. There is a strip of territory comprising possibly three hundred square miles north of Centreville that this road would serve that is now not served at all by any railway for at least four months in the year. It is a very serious situation, and possibly I can make plain to the minister and the House just what I mean. That section of New Brunswick lying west of the St. John river, between the St. John river and the American boundary and north of Centreville, is the section I refer to. During about four months of the year the farmers and producers cannot reach the Canadian Pacific without an extremely long haul. There is a bridge spanning the St. John river at Florenceville, and another at Andover. Between these two points the Canadian Pacific railway follows the eastern side of the St. John river. It is a mighty river and there are two months in the fall, when the ice is forming when farmers cannot cross with their teams. That is the time of the year when the farmers need to sell their produce in order to meet the bills coming due about the first of January. But that is the time, between the completion of their fall work and the beginning of the year when it is almost impossible for them to cross the river. The same condition obtains in the spring months when the ice begins to get poor-there is no crossing. It is a mighty river in the spring, and the freshets at that time, and the running logs, aggravate the situation. Possibly it is the middle of Majq sometimes the first of June, before it is possible for the ferry
boats to cross with teams with full loads. By that time the farmer has got into his spring work, and any potatoes he may have carried over will have deteriorated and not be fit for market. It is a serious situation for that section of the country, which I think is rightly called the garden of the province, so far at least as agriculture is concerned. It is all settled, the farmers having developed a fine agricultural area out of the forest against very adverse conditions. By reason of the fact that the road under discussion has not been completed a large number of the farmers have sold their holdings fairly cheap, being at a disadvantage in marketing their produce.
One of the reasons for the deficit on the St. John and Quebec railway is the fact that this extension of the road has not been built. This means that the traffic that should go over this road must go to the Canadian Pacific Railway at a time of year when it is most inconvenient for the farmers to market their stuff. Some years ago I was on a delegation which waited upon the government of the province of New Brunswick to urge the completion of the northern section of the road from Centreville to Grand Falls, and two arguments against the work were advanced at that time. One was the fact that the cost of construction was too high to warrant it; and the other was that we had no connection with the Maine Central, being more or less held up both for empty cars coming in and by the freight rate of the Canadian Pacific, who had control of that section of the road between Vanceboro and Fredericton and Vanceboro and St. John. It meant that if this connecting link were not built we were merely a collecting agency for freight for the Canadian Pacific. In fact, the Premier of New Brunswick, at that time Hon. W. E. Foster, told us that if we could induce the Dominion government to build the connecting link between the St. John and Quebec road and the Maine Central the province would have no hesitation in completing the northern section of the St. John and Quebec railway with the assistance of the Dominion subsidy. I was a very new member at Ottawa at that time, but I arranged an interview with the then Minister of Railways, Dr. Reid, at which the president of the St. John and Quebec Railway and the president of the Eastern Maine Railway Company, so-called, were also present. They came to an understanding with Dr. Reid that he would bring down a bill the next year to complete this connecting link. The next year, however, when the railway report was submitted to parliament it disclosed an immense railway deficit and Dr. Reid refused to bring

St. John and Quebec Railway
down this promised bill. He declared, and rightly so perhaps, that the deficit was too high to allow him to take up the matter and he did not feel like introducing the bill. The present Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) has brought down a bill for this purpose on two occasions and has piloted it through this House, I must say with very strong opposition from at least one of the members for St. John, who gave as a reason for opposing the proposition that it would hurt the port of St. John. I have never agreed with this contention, for I do not think that this connecting link would divert any traffic from St. John; I cannot see how it would, because there is no traffic to-day going through the port of St. John that would not still take that route if this link were built. The completion of this section would simply mean that traffic over the Intercolonial railway destined to New England points would go over the Canadian Government railway to Vaneeboro instead of over the Canadian Pacific.
I hope there will be no opposition to this bill. I have it on good authority from the powers that be in New Brunswick that they do propose to go ahead with their portion of the undertaking and they sincerely hope that the Dominion government will do its part. I think it is the only logical thing for the government to do. With the road in its present position, losing for the Dominion government a quarter of a million a year and for the provincial government a quarter of a million, it means that in eight years this combined loss would amount to four million dollars, which would be enough to complete the road and turn it into an asset, whereas at the present time it is merely a liability. It is my candid opinion that if the road were completed to Grand Falls to connect with the Transcontinental at that point, and the connecting link from Kingsclear to Vaneeboro, or possibly Harvey, and then over the Canadian Pacific Railway from that point, would not only pay operating costs and interest on cost of construction but would also eventually pay the capital cost. I am well convinced of that fact, and living in that immediate vicinity I have a very good idea of the whole situation. I trust, therefore, that the bill providing for this extension will pass.
Resolution reported read the second time and concurred in. speechtext:
Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend The Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act, chapter 18 of the statutes of 1923, by making provisions,
(a)	to facilitate business on the stock yards by providing that all moneys received on account of sales for live stock sold by a commission firm on behalf of the owner thereof shall be deposited in a shipper's live stock commission account instead of a shipper's trust account as at present;
(b)	to provide for the licensing of egg buyers, egg collectors and dealers, and exporters of live stock, meat, poultry, eggs and wool;
(c)	to amend the power to make regulations as to the manner in which eggs found to be unfit for human consumption shall be valued and disposed of.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair:
On paragraph (a):

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Most of the farmer members will recall that prior to two years ago there was a good deal of complaint that, when stockyard buyers went out into the country purchasing animals and giving cheques for them, it was found that in some instances when the cheques went back to the bank, they were not honoured. Usually there was money when the man started out buying, but perhaps the bank found there was some other claim upon the party and it would appropriate the bank account for its own or the other party's use. Consequently an attempt was made two years ago to provide against this contingency by having all moneys used for purchasing cattle deposited to the credit of the buyer in what is called a trust account which could be devoted to that purpose only. This was intended to correct the difficulty complained of, but it was found that it could not be corrected in that way without violating the usual practices in the administration of trust accounts. The legal authorities contend that when an animal is sold to a buyer, the money that can be used for buying that animal cannot be used until the animal is resold by the buyer and the money placed in that trust account. That is impossible and the difficulty has not been remedied. Consequently, instead of the buyer having his money placed in a trust account out of which it seems to be difficult to get it for the purpose desired, the legal authorities advise that it is better to place the money in

Live Stock Products Act
a shipper's live stock commission account and then it will effect its purpose. That is the purpose of paragraph (a) of the resolution, and it gets over the difficulty of the trust account which we found was not very much better than the old method. There have been no great complaints under the trust account method, but if the procedure had ever been challenged, it would be found that we were violating the usual procedure under trust accounts. That is the reason why we are making this change.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Does that embrace moneys received from co-operative shipments? Are they deposited in shippers' accounts and then the cheques made out to the individuals who have built up the co-operative shipments?

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT

I do not think
there has been any difficulty in connection with that. We have been trying out this trust account method but we have been violating another phase of the law to do so.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I asked the question because, in the past, individuals to whom co-operative shipments have been sent have deposited the proceeds of the shipments to their private account, and sometimes, as a result, the individuals who built up the co-operative shipment have not received their money.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
This will correct
that.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Will this be referred to the Agricultural committee also?

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes. All these bills will be.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I have had one of those cheques such as the minister describes deposited in one of my pigeonholes at home for six or eight years. Many that should have gone to me went to the bank. I hope sufficient protection will be provided by this amendment.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Has the minister considered the use of certified cheques? That would seem to me to be a very simple method of securing payment to the owner of the cattle. Such cheques could be paid only to the order of the person who holds the cheque and funds are retained for that purpose.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: In that case every cheque would have to be certified and the man would have to be at the bank to get a certified cheque. That would correct the difficulty only for one particular cheque.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not see where the proposal in this resolution is going to deal
with the buyer at all. This refers entirely to the commission man. If a man is going out buying cattle, he would be just as free under this resolution to give a man a worthless cheque as he is now.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Anybody can give
a worthless cheque if he likes to take the risk, but this is to prevent the practice, which was rather common in days past, of a bank taking over and charging up any overdue notes to a man's bank account as
4 p.m. is the usual practice. If you give a note to a bank and you do not settle it at maturity, it will be charged up to your account. That might absorb all the balance that was in the account and there would be nothing to honour the cheques that come in. This is to provide a separate account altogether from a man's private account.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: A commission account only?

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is the point. If
the man is buying stock, this does not affect him at all. If he is a commission man handling on commission, it would affect him.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I went all through
this two years ago and the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) was good enough to assist me. We were all in a quandary and I consulted with my hon. friend. I give him credit for suggesting to me what we both thought was good advice, and we tried it out. The lawyers in the House did not seem to be able to offer any solution. My hon. friend was a banker and we worked this method out together, but we ran up against another difficulty and this is to get over it.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: If the minister had consulted the lawyer members in the first place, he would not have run up against this difficulty

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Perhaps not.
Lawyers are useful sometimes.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Since the minister has
mentioned my name-

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am not complaining; I think we both thought it was all right.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I still think the act as it
stands now is all right. Possibly it is causing a little trouble for the commission man, putting him to a little extra bother, and that is why they are asking for a change. The act as it stands now, compelling the commission man to deposit the money in a trust account, is making the money of the owner of the cattle
Live Stock Products Act

safer than it will be when it is simply carried in a special live stock commission account. Under the act as it stands now, if a commission man used that money for any other purpose, he would be violating a trust. At the same time it .prevents the bank charging up any note which the man might owe the bank, to his trust account. The minister is quite correct in stating that this was done formerly, and it was the cause of the present act being passed two years ago. There were certain commission firms in Calgary and Winnipeg that had lost money through the buying and selling of cattle. They were in debt to the bank. AVhen a large shipment of cattle was received by the commission firm it deposited the proceeds of sale in the bank and issued a check to the owner of the cattle, but before the latter could get his cheque cashed the bank had charged up the firm's note. They had really taken the proceeds of the man's cattle to pay the commission firm's debt to the hank-a very unfair and, I think, dishonest practice. The present law absolutely prohibits that practice. So far as I can see, the amendment is being made to meet the wishes of the commission men who are put to some bother through the working of the present act. I wrote the Western Stock Growers' Association for their views on the change proposed by the minister, they did not offer any objection to it, so personally I am not going to object to the bill going to committee. I took this matter up in the first- place at the request of that association and did my best to get some law enacted that would protect the shippers of cattle. I believe that as the law stands we have that protection, and the commission men have got along with it for two years. Therefore I think when this resolution goes to the committee on Agriculture the commission men, or whoever are advocating the change, should be required to show why the present act should be changed, for I am sure it is protecting the shippers.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I can assure the
committee, Mr. Chairman, that all these phases will be threshed out and everybody will be given an opportunity before the agricultural committee to discuss the amendments so we may get everything just right. Sometimes in curing one difficulty we create another, and this we want to avoid. But the tanning business does not absorb them all. and we want to make regulations so that the surplus may be destroyed in an incinerator or in some other way to be prescribed. We find that some unscrupulous persons, taking advantage of the regulations which permit five offgrade eggs to a case, will substitute this number of bad eggs and make a corresponding profit. Supply-Marine and Fisheries

speakeroldname: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext:
Perhaps I might as well
read the statement with regard to this vote:
This proposed appropriation is for the continuance of operations in connection with the deepening and widening of the St. Lawrence ship channel between Montreal and Father Point, and for the enlargement and acceleration of these operations.
Provision was made in the main estimates for the fiscal year 1924-25 for $613,000 for the maintenance and operation of the fleet then in commission, and in the supplementary estimates an additional amount of $350,000 was voted for the reconditioning of additional vessels which had been laid up for some years, with the view to the enlargement of operations next season.
The amount required to maintain and operate the enlarged fleet next season is estimated at $1,010,000, which includes $200,000 for night operations. Provision is also made for the expenditure of $653,000 in the reconditioning of vessels laid up, additional to those for which provision was made in the supplementary estimates last year, and for the construction of several new vessels.
Previous to the war a large expenditure was made in maintaining, deepening and widening the St. Lawrence ship channel from Montreal to Father Point, but on account of the war a number of the vessels and dredges were laid off and anchored in Sorel harbour, and the greater part of the work was stopped. Since the war we have been taking the work up again little by little. It was first planned to deepen the St. Lawrence ship channel to 30 feet, but about 1910, the programme was changed and it was decided to make it a 35-foot channel. This work has not been started in order particularly to help Montreal or any other port in the province of Quebec, but with the sole object of developing this very important shipping route, known as the St. Lawrence route, and I think it is in the national interest that the work should be undertaken and carried on. Besides, we are receiving and have been receiving for a long time complaints from the shipping companies and the Pilots' Association in regard to the condition of the St. Lawrence, and even when we shall have placed in commission all the dredges which were in operation before the war, it will still take about ten years before the programme of deepening the St. Lawrence to 35 feet is completed. It is most important that we should carry on this dredging. Its importance has been recognized by all previous governments, and large amounts of money have been spent on it. Having taken that into consideration, and in view of the various representations which have been made to my department by the shipping companies and different other interests, I think this government is justified in spending a little larger amount this year than was spent last

year, particularly in view of the fact that with the best intentions and even with this enlarged expenditure the programme cannot be completed before ten years.
Mr. GARLAND (Bow River:) Just how is this work being done? Is it being done, by sections, gradually spreading over the whole route?

The work is divided into five sections: (1) from Montreal to Sorel, 45 miles; (2) from Sorel to Batiscan, 36 miles, not including lake St. Peter; (3) lake St. Peter, 20 miles; (4) Batiscan to Quebec, 59 miles; (5) Quebec to Goose Cape, 66 miles.

What I
really want to get at is whether the work is being done over the whole route at the same moment.
Yes.

What
special need has arisen for this great depth? Are the boats coming up the St. Lawrence becoming larger all the time?

Yes, the tendency is always to increase the capacity of the boats. But even for the ordinary shipping, we find it is absolutely necessary to have this dredging carried on, in order that it shall be known to all that the St. Lawrence ship channel is perfectly safe, and that nobody shall have reason to complain about it. We often hear complaints about the insurance rates on cargoes and ships, and I think it is in the interest of the whole of Canada that the St. Lawrence ship channel be put in such a condition that we shall be in a position to ask for a reduction of insurance rates. The greater the depth, the safer the ship travelling along this very important route.

Are there to be more
dredges put on, or are the present ones going to do additional work?

We are putting more dredges into commission. They are not new ones, as they were operated before the war, but were laid up during the period of war. We have had repairs made to a certain number of these dredges which we are now placing in commission, and we intend to maintain double shifts on duty, so that the work will be carried on night and day.

The minister says the larger boats are coming to Quebec, and therefore the necessity for this dredging. Might I ask if the dredging is not continued on up to Montreal?

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
Yes.
Is the new system of piloting by means of a cable on the bottom of the channel being used on the St. Lawrence ship channel?
No.

Of course,
I am not specially interested in either Montreal or Quebec. I would not wish any favouritism shown to the one as against the other, but I would like to have the minister explain why he believes it to be in the national interest that these larger boats should be able to come up to Montreal. Why is this additional amount of work necessary? Would it not do if the channel was deepened from Father Point to Quebec, and the boats loaded and unloaded at that port? We find Quebec a good port for our live stock.

I am quite free to admit
that the port of Quebec is a good one, and I say here it needs to be given all the assistance we can give it, but we must also remember the investment that has been made in the port of Montreal, the organizations that are established there, and its great importance as a shipping point. It is necessary to keep Montreal in line with the developments that are going on elsewhere. I might point out here that the dredging is not simply carried on from Quebec to Montreal, but also from Quebec to Goose Cape. Up to two or three years ago the vessels have been using what we call the south channel, passing on the south side of Grosse Isle, but for several years past, the department has been engaged in deepening the channel on the north side of Grosse Isle, and this channel has been found more advantageous by a great number of ships. The shipping companies are anxious now to have this channel completed, and quite a sum of the amount asked for by this item of 'the estimates is to be expended in deepening what we call the north channel. Although the dredging we are carrying on will no doubt facilitate entry to the port of Quebec, we have also to maintain the whole channel which has been deepened at a very large expenditure in the past, because even in developing the port of Quebec to its full capacity and giving it all the advantages we could, there are still a certain number of vessels that would likely come up to Montreal, on account of its importance as a shipping centre and on account of the commercial establishments that are to be found there.

If this $700,000 was not
spent, will the minister take the responsibility
of saying that shipping would not get along just as well this year as it did last year? My point is that the discussion during the last few months in parliament and the attitude of the public is in favour of the most rigid economy, and to expend $700,000 on dredging, with our finances as they are, is something which I think will cause a great question mark to arise in the mind of the public throughout Canada unless the minister can give adequate reasons justifying this expenditure. I again ask him, will he say on his responsibility that shipping could not continue for another year without a part of this $700,000 being expended?

I am quite free to admit
that the ships would likely continue to come up to Montreal with the channel as it is at the present time, but we have to take into consideration the numerous complaints that have been made to the department, about the channel not being in the condition it should be in. If the channel is not deep enough, it is just that much more dangerous, and it gives a reason to the insurance companies to still maintain their present high rates in force. The St. Lawrence route is in reality under a handicap in comparison with other routes to American ports, and we are receiving complaints that it is not as safe as these other routes.

May I ask the source of
these complaints and whether they are serious in their nature? Are they merely the complaints of people who are always wanting something done?

These are not complaints
from people who merely wish to see money expended. The representatives of the shipping federation at Montreal often come to my office and complain about the situation. The trading organizations in that city have been doing the same thing; and the pilots, who steer the ships from Quebec to Montreal complain very often about existing conditions. Very frequently last year, in the closing days of the season of navigation, vessels left the port of Montreal with only two or three feet of water under their hulls. If this is not an adequate reason for placing the channel in a safe condition, I am at a loss to know what would be a good reason.

Is that the only available
channel, or is it possible to take some other route?

It is the only available channel; there is no other route.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

What is the ordinary depth
of the channel?	,

The average. I think, is
twenty-nine feet and a fraction.

What are you making the
depth of the channel now?
Thirty-five feet. A certain part of the channel has a depth of thirty feet at present, but our programme is to deepen it to thirty-five feet.
Is this work being done by government outfits, or is it being carried out by outside parties under contract?
It is being done by government outfits. All these dredges are the property of the government.

Can the minister tell us
what amount of filling-in takes place through the deposit of silt or other material in the channel?
I am informed that there is only one place where filling-in to any extent has occurred, and that is not very far from Three Rivers.
What period of time will be occupied in deepening the channel to a depth of thirty-five feet?
With the appropriation we are asking now, and the carrying on of the work in the manner we contemplate, it will take ten years before we reach completion.
With the full amount of 81,600.000 each year?
Yes.
Does the minister anticipate any increase in the vote? In other words, will the minister give the committee his present estimate of what the total cost of the work will be?
Well, if it is taken for granted that it will take ten years to complete the work it is only necessary to multiply the present amount by ten.

Can the minister give the committee the cost of the work for the years 1921, 1922 and 1923? While he is looking up the information may I say that I hesitate to think of what is going to happen to the finances of the country by the time we reach Toronto.
Perhaps we will continue to Hudson bay then.

Frankly T do not think the country is in a position to face an expenditure of this kind. I have no objection to a moderate amount of work being done in deepening the channel a few feet in order to make it safer, but to go down to a depth of thirty-five feet all along the line would seem to me to require further justification than the minister has been able to give us. I should like him to tell us just what the ratio of increase in the draught of boats has been in the last four years, and what the anticipated increase in draught will be in the next ten years, that will justify deepening the channel to thirty-five feet. How much larger does the minister expect vessels using this channel to become?

Surely my hon. friend does not think I am in a position to say how
much larger ocean vessels may become-
But we are spending all this money.

-in ten years or even in
one year; we do not know -that. But even with the present capacity of ocean vessels we are receiving complaints that the channel is not sufficiently deep and there is a liability of accidents, of a large vessel being stranded with the result of completely blocking the channel. In what position would the government or the department be placed if, as a result of the channel not being sufficiently wide or sufficiently deep-one of these large vessels leaving Montreal with only -two or three feet of water under its hull went considerably out of its course in a. channel only five hundred feet wide? In what position would either the government or the department. find itself if such an accident happened in consequence of the complaints and representations of shipping companies and other concerns being ignored? We want to avoid such a calamity. We want -to make sure that navigation on the St. Lawrence route is made safe, and that neither that route nor our country will be discriminated against because of failure to make navigation as safe as we can make it.

The minister is to be congratulated on the view he takes with which I agree entirely. But that is not the point. The point is, just what

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
depth and breadth does he consider this channel should have, and the reason therefor?

Several years ago, I think it was in 1910, it was decided that the depth of the channel should be thirty-five feet. Careful inquiries have been made, the question has been thoroughly discussed with the various interests concerned, and it has been deemed necessary to proceed with the work so that there might be a uniform depth, in the channel, of thirty-five feet, instead of thirty feet. The expenditure, in our opinion, is justified by the importance of the work and the advantages that will accrue not only to the shipping interests, but to the country at large from the deepening of the channel.

The expenditure proposed
to be made on this work in the next ten years will amount to $16,630,000. Will this work when completed form part of the international scheme for the improvement of the waterways?

It will certainly be an
essential part of it.
The contemplated width and depth of the channel will be in conformity with the plans contemplated for the improvement of the international waterway?
Certainly.
This work will be considered as part of the Canadian programme?

It can be considered as a
Canadian contribution.

That is the objective of
the department at the present time?

I am not in a position
to say that we are doing this work at the present time as part of our share in the undertaking, but it will be in harmony with the scheme which is contemplated.

I should like to
ask the minister a question for the purpose of getting some information. In the recent past there has been a good deal of controversy between Canada and the United States and between different sections in the United States in regard to the Chicago drainage canal and the lowering of the lake level. According to what I have read, some have gone so far as to state that lake levels have been considerably lowered in the last few years because of the action of the Chicago authorities in draining off the water in lake Michigan. Does this affect the water level of the St. Lawrence? Taking a period of some three of four years back, has the minister any
information to give the committee regarding the level of the St. Lawrence?

There has no doubt been
a reduction in the level of the St. Lawrence because of the condition referred to, but it is difficult to determine exactly the extent to which this has taken place. We are, however, under the impression that the level has been affected.

To what
extent, approximately?
It is a matter of inches.

It seems to me that if it does affect the level of the St. Lawrence to any extent whatever, this should be used as an additional argument by the Canadian authorities against any diversion by the Chicago drainage canal. So far as I have read, I have not seen such an argument advanced up to date, and I think it would be effective.

Does the minister think that there is any advantage in spending public money to any greater extent than is productive of good business in the development of a trade route? The figures I have before me show that something like $17,000,000 has been spent in the dredging of the St. Lawrence ship channel up to the present time; and with the $16,000,000 odd which it is intended to spend in the next ten years there will have been put into this channel over $30,000,000, apart from lights, buoys and all other necessaries. I am wondering whether it pays to develop any trade route if it is too costly. Might it not be better for the ships to go as far as Quebec?

We all agree that the port of Quebec should be developed, and the necessary dredging to facilitate the entry of ships into that port should be done. At the same time we must take care of the St. Lawrence channel from Quebec to Montreal, because there will always be a certain number of vessels going to Montreal, in view of the large commercial and industrial establishments that carry on business there. And the hon. member knows that water transportation is always cheaper than railway hauling, so that the further inland we can go by water, the better it will be for our trade. I am sure that the money expended on the St. Lawrence route has been spent to great advantage, because in the proper sense of the term the St. Lawrence ship channel is a national utility. I do not think, therefore, that it would be wise to stop the work there at the present time.
Supply-Marine and Fisheries

No one will object to
maintaining the present channel from Quebec to Montreal, but the question is, shall we save enough in the water transportation over the rail haul to compensate for the cost of deepening and maintaining that waterway?
We think it will be a great saving; it is the natural course.

This discussion is interesting in view of the proposed arrangement between the Dominion and the government of the United States for the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway to the head of the Great Lakes; and as this question has come up regarding the immense cost of keeping the channel open as far as Montreal, I think the government might well pause before spending any money even for investigating the feasibility of carrying out the scheme for deepening the waterway to the head of the lakes. It is and always has been my opinion that the time has not yet come when that should even be considered. If our present transportation system will not handle the traffic from western and central Canada to the seaboard, then the time may come when this undertaking may be necessary. But I think it is so far ahead of present requirements that not a dollar should be spent even in investigating the project at the present time. I quite agree that it is necessary to keep the ship channel at the proper depth as far as Montreal for the type of vessels that go to that port, but I think, although I am subject to correction in this regard, that the port of Quebec is nearer to Winnipeg by rail than is the port of Montreal. The Transcontinental runs by such a direct route that, according to my information, the mileage is less between Winnipeg and Quebec than between Winnipeg and Montreal. The government might, therefore, well consider the advisability of using the National Transcontinental for the purpose for which we were told it was built. If that were done, moreover, the haul would be shorter from Winnipeg to St. John via Quebec than from Winnipeg to Portland via Montreal. This government proposes to develop the Canadian ports east and west, and this is commendable. And this I think is one of the methods towards that end. The Transcontinental has never been used to capacity, although it has a better grade than any other road in Canada and is capable of hauling larger trains than any of the other roads in the Dominion. The route, I repeat, is shorter to Quebec and if it were adopted it would obviate the necessity of deepening the channel between the harbour of 
Quebec and the harbour of Montreal to any greater extent than at the present time. This is my firm opinon on this matter, and I thought this an opportune time to express it,
Mr. McCONI'CA:	The complaint, as I
understand it, is that they are only bringing in cargoes to about forty per cent capacity and taking out eighty per cent, and I do not see that there is any immediate necessity for deepening this river. And in any case, it strikes me that it might be better to make boats fit the river than to make the river fit the boats.

The St. Lawrence route
is not the main part of their trip. They have to navigate deeper waters than those of the St. Lawrence. The St. Lawrence constitutes only a small portion of their trip and we cannot control the capacity of a boat to be in accordance with the channel of the St Lawrence. We have to accept the boats which are now navigating the oceans.
After this ten-year programme is carried out and all this dredging is done, will it be necessary to continue dredging to maintain the channel to a depth of thirty-five feet?

No further dredging will
be necessary.
How many miles of dredging are involved now?

On the thirty-five foot
programme, there are eighty-one miles requiring dredging.

Has the dredging so far
been conducted on the basis of a thirty-five foot channel? That is to say, has it not been conducted on the basis of a thirty-foot channel prior to date?
No.
There has been no dredging below the thirty feet?

Yes. On the first division
from Montreal to Sorel, twenty miles have been dredged to thirty-five feet.
When was that done?

This work was started in
1910 and it has been continued since then.

How many miles are
dredged to that depth now?
Forty-five miles.

I was very much in
terested in the point raised by the hon. mem

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
ber for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael). It has a very direct bearing on this question of dredging the St. Lawrence channel. What steps have the government taken to check the diversion of water by the Chicago drainage canal, and do they hope to effect any check on that by negotiations that 5 p,m. are now under way, or, if not, do they propose to take any more drastic measures? It is a very serious matter to this country if a foreign power is to be allowed to divert our water and if we must continue to dredge this channel deeper and deeper as time goes on, because I think it is a well known fact that the deeper you go the harder the dredging is. You get down to hard pan which is more difficult to dredge than the ordinary bottom of the river.

Steps have been taken, not by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, but by the Department of the Interior. The Minister of the Interior has been dealing with this question. The only thing that we did in the Department of Marine and Fisheries was to lend to the Department of the Interior the late Mr. Stewart, who died recently. He was head of the Hydrographic Survey in the Department of Marine and Fisheries and he worked with the Department of the Interior in connection with their dealings with the United States. The Marine department has nothing to do in regard to that.
Is it a fact, as has been suggested by the hon. member for Kindersley, that this lessening of the flow has not been put up as part of the case against the diversion of water?
I should think it has been made a part of the protest because the late Mr. Stewart was quite conversant with all these things.
The minister should make a note of that and if it has not been stressed, it should be stressed as the main argument.
I will certainly make a note of it, but I am quite convinced it has been done.

Is all the work in connection with the construction and maintenance of the St. Lawrence ship channel carried on by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, or is there any overlapping by the Department of Public Works?

This work is carried on
by the Department of Marine and Fisheries only.

The Department of
Public Works does some dredging on the St. Lawrence, it may be in harbours?
Not in relation to the channel.

What is their part of
the dredging?

Deepening the water in
front of wharves. They never work in the channel. Their work is always outside of the main channel.

It is the dredging of
harbours?
Yes.

Do the minister and
the government not think this dredging, especially in the one river, should all be done under one department? I can well understand if you were going to Hudson bay, you would have to send some other department you had no use for, so that if they got frozen in during the winter you would not miss them; but as regards dredging rivers like the St. Lawrence, I would strongly urge having this all under one department. This has been urged repeatedly, but no attention seems to be paid to it. Every minister admits that this should be done, but evidently he forgets all about it or there is no co-ordination. I realize possibly as well as anybody the difficulty of co-ordinating under one head work that has become split up into several sections; but the government should very seriously consider at this time co-ordinating this work and cutting out duplication of expenditure. I do not want to steal the theme of the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) as regards cutting out duplication of service, but this is one place where it might very well be put into practice.

What is the estimated cost
per mile from the international point of view of constructing the channel?
The work is estimated, no on a mileage basis, but on a cubic yarc basis.

I understand this is part of a
programme commenced in 1910. I observe that the estimate for last year was $613,000 and for the previous year, $613,000. Was the work in those years part of the programme started in 1910? Where was the dredging done and to what extent during those years? What was the average cost per mile?

During last year dredging
was done to the extent of 1,373,420 cubic

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
yards at an average cost of 66-2 cents per cubic yard.
If the minister could put that in miles one would understand it better. Was it thirty feet before, or twenty-eight, or what?

The average depth is
twenty-nine feet and a fraction.
Was that the depth when the programme was instituted in 1910, and the programme involved dredging the channel to a depth of thirty-five feet?
Yes.
Can the minister tell us how many miles have been dredged in the last three years?
In 1924, on the thirty-five foot project, we dredged 128 miles at varying depths.
How much the year before?

The question of giving British Columbia larger representation on the board is under consideration and will be taken up at the next meeting of the board.

I did not catch the
name of the British Columbia representative.
He is Mr. Dybhaven.
Is he a scientific man?
He is representing industry, I am informed.

That does not touch
the point at all. As I understand it we were to have a scientific man on the coast who would devote his whole time to studying the habits of the fish, the possibility of restoring the run of salmon on the Fraser river and other matters connected with the Pacific coast fisheries. The minister knows how important the matter is particularly in regard to the Fraser river. The minister no doubt is aware that a few years ago we had a run of salmon on the Fraser river which brought in something like 900,000 cases of salmon per year. That run has been depleted so that at the present time it amounts to simply a matter of fifty or sixty thousand cases or so a year. In consequence the loss to the country is enormous. The matter to be looked into and

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
investigated is whether something can be done to restore the run of sockeye salmon on the Fraser river. Who is going to do that? It is not a matter for some man who is engaged in industry but for a scientific authority; one who will devote all his time to the work, and not a university professor who will simply employ part of his vacation for the purpose. I think the department is derelict if it does not make arrangements to carry out the promise which was given to us. We cannot play with this question. I do not think the minister is anxious to play with it as he must appreciate its importance. In connection with the Fraser river there are various matters that have to be taken into consideration. One of these, of course, is whether or not it is possible to make some arrangement with the fisheries board of the state of Washington. There must be co-operation between the authorities of the state of Washington and our government if anything permanent is to be achieved. I should like to ask the minister also what is the present state of the negotiations with the state of Washington authorities as to the Fraser river. I understand, and no doubt the minister has the necessary particulars, that some negotiations have been carried on, and that a joint committee has been appointed composed of representatives of the state of Washington and of the Canadian Department of Marine and Fisheries. It would be interesting in fact I think it is necessary, to know what is going on in this connection.

The situation at present is more encouraging than it has ever been before. The negotiations that are being carried on are quite satisfactory and the department is hopeful that the results Obtained will be equally gratifying. No definite decision has been reached so far. As regards the employment of an experienced man to look into the question of the restoration of the fisheries on the Fraser river, Dr. Forester is devoting his time to a study of the matter. The biological board, at its next meeting, will consider the question of increasing the number of its members and, if a decision is reached, the request of my hon. friend, to appoint someone with a special knowledge of conditions there, will no doubt foe taken into consideration.
What are Dr. Forester's qualifications?

He is well known as a
scientist and has been recommended by the biological board.
Where is he located?

He is attached to the
station at Nanaimo, under Dr. Clemens.
That is hardly studying the Fraser river.
This is his particular work ; he is looking particularly into the Fraser river situation.

But the minister says that he is at Nanaimo. What investigation is he carrying on? I am not asking these questions merely for the sake of taking up the time of the committee. The matter is an important one, as the minister must realize.

I quite understand the importance of the subject. I understand that he has been carrying on an investigation on the Fraser river for quite a while.
Mr. MicQUARRIE:	Has he been actually
on the Fraser river?

Yes.

furnish the committee with any details as to what investigations he has carried on?

He is supposed to make
reports to the biological board, who in turn will report to the department.

Over two years ago.
M:r. McQUARRIE: And has he not made any report yet?

No report has been made
to the department, but .possibly he has reported or given information to the biological board. So far the department has received no information from the board.
I submit that the department should be interested in the matter.
The department is, indeed.

Then I think that the
department should ascertain what reports Dr. Forester has made to the board, and we should have the details of them. Surely there is not much object in having a man make investigations unless some action is to be taken or unless we can know what reports he submits.

These investigations must
necessarily cover a long period; he cannot report every few months.

But he has had two
years now in which to study the situation. I admit that there are a number of matters

which will need to be investigated. There is for instance the matter of hatcheries, which has been referred to. I do not say that I am in favour of doing away with hatcheries; as a matter of fact, from my study of many years of hatchery methods, I thought that some improvement might be made in connection with the hatcheries of this country. But I have never advocated that the hatchery system should be discontinued, for I do not believe that this would be wise. Then there is the matter of the enemies of the salmon; for instance, the hair seal. This is a subject that must be studied. The hair seal at present destroys more salmon than the fishermen can catch. The fishermen have great difficulties to contend with in bringing in their fish, which are caught in the nets, before the seal can destroy them. There is also the danger from trout, which destroy the salmon spawn. Then there is the question of the restoration of the spawning grounds, thousands of acres of which, in the upper reaches of the Fraser river, have been entirely depleted, 'being now barren. Are these spawning grounds going to be restored? If you cannot restore them and get the fish to go there and spawn, then of course the run of sock-eye salmon will never be restored. What I want to know is whether this matter is being taken up seriously, or whether it has simply been handed over to Dr. Forester, who is looking into it and will perhaps in the dim and distant future submit some report which will be pigeon-holed. Is this what will happen, or do we intend to get down to business and see whether something practical cannot be accomplished? I must say, I am not satisfied with the information which the minister has given us to-night, and I really think the department should show more interest in the subject.

I may explain that this
biological station is not at Nanaimo but at Departure Bay, which is in the district of Comox-Albemi. I visited it last fall, but I am sorry to say that my memory is not sufficiently vivid to enable me to describe exactly wffiat investigation they were carrying out. Dr. Clemens was not there, but I met his assistant, who showed me over the grounds and explained carefully the kind of work he was going in for and the methods employed. I can only say, speaking in a general way, that I was favourably impressed with the economy and the efficiency with which the station was being run, and with the fact that there was being carried on a work of a thoroughly useful character.	I am sorry I
cannot state the precise work he was engaged
on, but the impression left on my mind was that we were getting good value for the money spent on that station.
